details: Cebel-i Demāvend: It lies on the frontier of Rey (modern Ray, Iran). At times it can be seen from Sāve (modern Saveh, Iran). The dome-shaped summit in the middle becomes visible. And at all times there is no lack of smoke rising from its top. Truly, no one has ever climbed to its very peak. According to some, the Prophet Süleymān—peace be upon him—confined the ṣaḫre jinn there. Likewise Efrīdūn imprisoned Ḍaḥḥāk there as well. It is related from Mis‘ar bin Mühelhil that he climbed up to half of it with a thousand hardships—though many times he nearly fell and perished. And he reached a fissure from which kibrīt-i aḥmer (red sulphur) flowed. All around it the substance solidified and froze. But when the sun rose, it would ignite and become a blazing fire. It is transmitted from the inhabitants of the villages on the mountain’s slopes that whenever ants swarm around Kūh-i Demāvend (modern Mount Damavand, Iran), famine and scarcity unfailingly appear in those regions. Whenever snow and rain fall continuously on the mountain’s skirts, the people of the surrounding lands pour goat’s milk upon the fire, and at that very moment they see the rain cease. And whenever one side of the snowcap on the mountain’s summit freezes, strife breaks out in the region on that side and blood is shed... [partial translation]
title: Cebel-i Demāvend

details: BASSORA, a city of Arabia Deserta, in the province of Eyraca Arabic, Asia, stands about 250 miles S. E. from Bagdad, and about 240 S. W. from Ispahan, in lat. 30, and E. long. 57, on the frontiers of Persia, about half a league from the Euphrates (which the Arabs call Scetel Areb, or the Arabic river) and on the confluence of that and the Tigris into the Persian Gulph. It is a modern city, built by order of Omar, the second caliph, in 636, to cut off the communication of the Persians with India. It is large and opulent, 12 miles in circumference, but hath nothing extraordinary in its buildings, public or private. It stands on such a sandy and stony ground that there grows nothing about it, especially as it never rains there. But there is a small river pretty near it which enriches the valley through which it passes to such a degree, that the Arabs make it one of the four Paradises of the East. And the inhabitants are supplied with water from the Euphrates by a canal able to carry vessels of 50 tons. It has a fortress at the mouth of it, to prevent strangers coming into it without leave. It stands about 45 miles from sea, but the tide rises near as much again above it quite to the castle of Gorno. (Seally, 1787, Vol. 1, entry Bassora)
title: Bassora

details: Ḥīretü’l-beyżā: This is also one of the cities of ‘Irāḳ (Iraq), lying about one farsakh from Kūfe (Kufa). In the age of ignorance (zamān-ı cāhiliyye), it was a highly prosperous place. When Münẕir bin Ümerā’i’l-Ḳays gained victory over his enemies in this town, he restored it and had great churches (kenā’is-i ‘aẓīme) built there. According to some, the town now called Necef (Najaf) stands on the site of this former settlement. Others say that it was located on the shore of the Baḥr-i Fārs (Persian Gulf); this, too, is reported. It is also narrated that when one of the Tübbā‘ of Yemen traveled toward Ḫorāsān (Khorasan), he halted at a certain spot for the night, and the next day constructed a town there and named it Ḥīre. It is said that the Ḳaṣr-ı Ḥavernaḳ (Palace of Khavarnaq) is also located there, which was the residence of Nu‘mān bin Münẕir. [translation]

details: Baḥr-i Fārs (Persian Gulf): It is a sea that emerges from the northern side of the Baḥr-i Hind (Indian Ocean). To the east of Mekrāntīz (Makran coast region), at the source of the Baḥr-i Fārs, it appears visibly like a mouth (dehān). Likewise, the city of ‘Ummān (Oman) is seen on the western side of this sea, and it too is discernible at its mouth, that is, its strait. From there it extends, running along the ‘Ummān (Oman) coast, and from ‘Abbādān (Abadan, Iran) to Mehrūbān (Mahrūbān, near modern Bushehr). Then it passes to Sīnīz (modern Bushehr/Old Siniz) and stretches southward until it reaches Ḫayyābe (Khabbah / Khaybah). From there it proceeds to Seyfü’l-baḥr (“the Sword of the Sea,” Fars coast), and to its east is Sīrāf (Siraf, Iran). From that point, it continues along broken mountain ranges and high desert passes and hills, and then, moving further east, it winds around to Ḥıṣn Ibn ‘Ammāre (Hisn Ibn ‘Ammāra) and reaches Hürmüz (Hormuz), which is the port of Kirmān (Kerman). After that, it stretches toward the southeastern direction, reaching the Makran coast and Ḳaṣṣatīz. [translation]
title: ʿUmmān

details: Taḥrīr-i Ṣūret-i Iḳlīm el-Me’ḫūẕe Min Ṣuveri’l-eḳālīm ma‘a Baḥrü’l-Fārs Der-tafṣīl-i Ḥudūd-i Vilāyet-i Mıṣr u Cifār el-Menḳūle Min Teḳāvīmi’l-emṣār: ... The land of Egpyt is located on the east of Arabian Peninsula. Its southern frontier reaches the bilād-ı Sūdān (lands of the Sudan), that is Nūbe (Nubia?) and the other non-tribes of dark faces, from whose direction the Nīl-i Mıṣr (Nile River) comes. And its northern boundary is the Baḥr-i Rūm (Mediterranean Sea), and from Refaḥ (Rafah) to ‘Arīş (‘Arish), Cifār, Ṭīne (Tine/Al-Tina), Dimyāṭ (Damietta), the coast of Reşīd (Rosetta/Rashid), and İskenderiyye (Alexandria); and passing between Alexandria it reaches Berḳa (Barqa/Cyrenaica). Its western boundary runs between Berḳa (Barqa) and İskenderiyye (Alexandria) to the Cenevīz sāḥili (Genoese coast) and Ẓahru’l-vāḥāt, joins the frontiers of Nūbe (Nubia?). As for its southern boundary, it extends from the borders of Nubia to the cultivated lands by the Baḥr-i Ḳulzüm (Red Sea), and finally reaches the Tīh-i Benī İsrā’īl. Then turning northward once again, it reaches the Baḥr-i Rūm (Mediterranean) and ends at the place called Refaḥ (Rafah) where we began.... And the eastern border of Egypt extends from Baḥr-i Ḳulzüm (Red Sea) to the vicinity of Usvān (Aswan), and to ‘Ayẕāb (Aidhab), Kuṣayr (Qusayr/Quseir), Kulzüm (Suez), and the Tīh-i Benī İsrā’īl... [partial translation]

details: Der-ta‘yīn-i Ḥudūd-ı Vilāyet-i Yemen (Determining the Boundaries of the Province of Yemen): Since these lands lie to the right (south) of the territory of Mekke (Mecca), they have been called Yemen. Likewise, Şām (Syria) lies to the north, and thus it has been designated by that name. In its essence, Yemen is a very vast and broad land. It lies opposite the territory of Berber (the Berber lands / North Africa). In ancient times, the distance between Yemen and the sea was great, and a mountain lay between them as a barrier. But one of the kings, wishing to exact vengeance upon some of his enemies, ordered that mountain to be cut open and excavated. As a result, the sea poured forth onto those coasts and caused the destruction of many peoples and nations. [translation]

details: Taḥrīr-i Ṣūret-i Iḳlīm el-Me’ḫūẕe Min Ṣuveri’l-eḳālīm ma‘a Baḥrü’l-Fārs Der-tafṣīl-i Ḥudūd-i Vilāyet-i Mıṣr u Cifār el-Menḳūle Min Teḳāvīmi’l-emṣār: ... The land of Egpyt is located on the east of Arabian Peninsula. Its southern frontier reaches the bilād-ı Sūdān (lands of the Sudan), that is Nūbe (Nubia?) and the other non-tribes of dark faces, from whose direction the Nīl-i Mıṣr (Nile River) comes. And its northern boundary is the Baḥr-i Rūm (Mediterranean Sea), and from Refaḥ (Rafah) to ‘Arīş (‘Arish), Cifār, Ṭīne (Tine/Al-Tina), Dimyāṭ (Damietta), the coast of Reşīd (Rosetta/Rashid), and İskenderiyye (Alexandria); and passing between Alexandria it reaches Berḳa (Barqa/Cyrenaica). Its western boundary runs between Berḳa (Barqa) and İskenderiyye (Alexandria) to the Cenevīz sāḥili (Genoese coast) and Ẓahru’l-vāḥāt, joins the frontiers of Nūbe (Nubia?). As for its southern boundary, it extends from the borders of Nubia to the cultivated lands by the Baḥr-i Ḳulzüm (Red Sea), and finally reaches the Tīh-i Benī İsrā’īl. Then turning northward once again, it reaches the Baḥr-i Rūm (Mediterranean) and ends at the place called Refaḥ (Rafah) where we began.... And the eastern border of Egypt extends from Baḥr-i Ḳulzüm (Red Sea) to the vicinity of Usvān (Aswan), and to ‘Ayẕāb (Aidhab), Kuṣayr (Qusayr/Quseir), Kulzüm (Suez), and the Tīh-i Benī İsrā’īl... [partial translation]

details: Taḥrīr-i Ṣūret-i Iḳlīm el-Me’ḫūẕe Min Ṣuveri’l-eḳālīm ma‘a Baḥrü’l-Fārs Der-tafṣīl-i Ḥudūd-i Vilāyet-i Mıṣr u Cifār el-Menḳūle Min Teḳāvīmi’l-emṣār: ... The land of Egpyt is located on the east of Arabian Peninsula. Its southern frontier reaches the bilād-ı Sūdān (lands of the Sudan), that is Nūbe (Nubia?) and the other non-tribes of dark faces, from whose direction the Nīl-i Mıṣr (Nile River) comes. And its northern boundary is the Baḥr-i Rūm (Mediterranean Sea), and from Refaḥ (Rafah) to ‘Arīş (‘Arish), Cifār, Ṭīne (Tine/Al-Tina), Dimyāṭ (Damietta), the coast of Reşīd (Rosetta/Rashid), and İskenderiyye (Alexandria); and passing between Alexandria it reaches Berḳa (Barqa/Cyrenaica). Its western boundary runs between Berḳa (Barqa) and İskenderiyye (Alexandria) to the Cenevīz sāḥili (Genoese coast) and Ẓahru’l-vāḥāt, joins the frontiers of Nūbe (Nubia?). As for its southern boundary, it extends from the borders of Nubia to the cultivated lands by the Baḥr-i Ḳulzüm (Red Sea), and finally reaches the Tīh-i Benī İsrā’īl. Then turning northward once again, it reaches the Baḥr-i Rūm (Mediterranean) and ends at the place called Refaḥ (Rafah) where we began.... And the eastern border of Egypt extends from Baḥr-i Ḳulzüm (Red Sea) to the vicinity of Usvān (Aswan), and to ‘Ayẕāb (Aidhab), Kuṣayr (Qusayr/Quseir), Kulzüm (Suez), and the Tīh-i Benī İsrā’īl... [partial translation]

details:
Cebelü’s-S̠elc, Cebelü’l-Lübnān, Cebel-i Ukām: These are three mountains contiguous with one another which, extending from south to north, appear as a single mountain range. The southern one, which lies near Ṣafed (modern Safed, Israel), is Cebel-i S̠elc. It stretches northward and passes beyond the city of Dımaşḳ (modern Damascus, Syria). The people of that region call it Cebel-i Süneyd [appears as Sebḳad in one of the manuscripts of this work]. After this extension, the mountain that faces the west of Ba‘albek (modern Baalbek, Lebanon) is called Cebel-i Lübnān (Mount Lebanon). Just as it passes beyond Ba‘albek and reaches the mountain lying to the east of Ṭrablūs-Şām (modern Tripoli, Lebanon), that mountain is called Cebel-i ‘Akkār—for ‘Akkār is the name of a fortress located on its summit, and by association it has given the mountain its fame.

After it continues northward and passes beyond Ṭrablūs (modern Tripoli, Lebanon), they give the name Cebel-i Ukām to the mountain that first reaches Ḥıṣnu’l-Ekrād, then Ḥimṣ (modern Homs, Syria), then Ḥamā (modern Hama, Syria), Shīrez (likely Shayzar?, Syria), and the borders of Efāmiyye (modern Apamea, Syria). Then, passing beyond that and continuing in extension, the mountain appearing opposite Cebel-i Ukām is called Cebel-i Şaḥşebū, meaning that it is named in attribution to the village of Şaḥşebū. This mentioned mountain passes by Ma‘arra, Sermīn (modern Sermīn, Syria), and the western side of Ba‘albek, and becomes connected to Cebel-i Rūm. Likewise, Cebel-i Ukām, extending northward, passes Mehveb, then through S̠uġūr, Bekkās, and Ḳayṣer, and reaches Anṭākiyye (modern Antakya, Turkey), where it terminates. Opposite this, there is yet another mountain, and the Nehr-i ‘Āṣī (the Orontes River) flows between the two of them. [translation]
title: Cebel-i S̠elc

details: Der-ḥudūd-i Filisṭīn: It is a large district, within which lie Beytü’l-maḳdis (Jerusalem), Ġazze (Gaza), and ‘Asḳalān (Ashkelon). Its western boundary runs from Refaḥ (Rafah) to Leccūn (Legio), and its width is two days’ journey, extending from Yāfā (Jaffa) to Erīḥā (Jericho). At present, Zuġar, the diyār-ı Lūṭ (the region of Lot, i.e., around the Dead Sea), as well as Cibāl and Şerrān (the Sharon plain) are all attached to Filisṭīn (Palestine). Its water comes from rainfall, except in Nāblus (Nablus), where there is running water. And the great cities of this ‘örfī (customary administrative) district are Beyt-i Maḳdis (Jerusalem), Ġazze (Gaza), and Remle (Ramla). Allāh knows the best. [translation]

details: Bālīs: It is a small town on the Furāt (Euphrates) belonging to Cünd Ḳınnesrīn (the district of Qinnasrīn), and serves as a river port. Merchants coming from Mıṣr (Egypt) and diyār-ı Şām (Bilād al-Shām / Greater Syria) would embark on their boats at that place. They would send their goods to Baġdād (Baghdad) from that station. When the Melikü’n-nāṣır Ṣalāḥa’d-dīn (Salah al-Din) came to power, the waters of the Euphrates receded from Bālīs. Because of this, Ebū Bekr bin Ḳıvām-ı Bālīsī (Abū Bekr b. Ḳivām al-Bālīsī), one of the ascetics, diverted a canal from the Euphrates to Bālīs. For a long time, the people of the region benefitted from it. Afterwards, that too fell into ruin, and the town of Bālīs became deserted. The people of Bālīs are known for lack of sense and stupidity. [translation]
title: Bālīs

details: Der-ḥudūd-i Filisṭīn (Within the borders of Palestine): A large district including Beytü’l-maḳdis (Jerusalem), Ġazze (Gaza), and ‘Asḳalān (Ashkelon). Its western boundary extends from Refaḥ (Rafah) to Leccūn, and its breadth from Yāfā (Jaffa) to Erīḥā (Jericho) is a journey of two days. Zughar, the land of Lūṭ (Lot), Cibāl (Jibāl), and Şerran (Sharrān) are all part of the territory of Filisṭīn (Palestine). Its waters come from rainfall, except in Nāblus, where there is running water. The big cities in this region are Beyt-i Maḳdis (Bayt al-Maqdis), Ġazze (Gaza), and Remle (Ramla). God knows the best.
title: Beytü’l-maḳdis

details: Beytü’l-maḳdis: It is what they call Ḳuds-i Şerīf (al-Quds al-Sharīf). Another of its names is Īliyā, and another is Şalem, which in the Hebrew language means “house of peace.” As for the mosque, its name is Ṣahyūn (Zion) and Zeytūn (Olive / Mount of Olives). The term Ḥarem (the Sanctuary / Haram) was applied to it only later. In sum, it is one of the cities of Filisṭīn (Palestine)... [partial translation]

details: Taḥrīr-i Ṣūret-i Iḳlīm el-Me’ḫūẕe Min Ṣuveri’l-eḳālīm ma‘a Baḥrü’l-Fārs Der-tafṣīl-i Ḥudūd-i Vilāyet-i Mıṣr u Cifār el-Menḳūle Min Teḳāvīmi’l-emṣār: ... The land of Egpyt is located on the east of Arabian Peninsula. Its southern frontier reaches the bilād-ı Sūdān (lands of the Sudan), that is Nūbe (Nubia?) and the other non-tribes of dark faces, from whose direction the Nīl-i Mıṣr (Nile River) comes. And its northern boundary is the Baḥr-i Rūm (Mediterranean Sea), and from Refaḥ (Rafah) to ‘Arīş (‘Arish), Cifār, Ṭīne (Tine/Al-Tina), Dimyāṭ (Damietta), the coast of Reşīd (Rosetta/Rashid), and İskenderiyye (Alexandria); and passing between Alexandria it reaches Berḳa (Barqa/Cyrenaica). Its western boundary runs between Berḳa (Barqa) and İskenderiyye (Alexandria) to the Cenevīz sāḥili (Genoese coast) and Ẓahru’l-vāḥāt, joins the frontiers of Nūbe (Nubia?). As for its southern boundary, it extends from the borders of Nubia to the cultivated lands by the Baḥr-i Ḳulzüm (Red Sea), and finally reaches the Tīh-i Benī İsrā’īl. Then turning northward once again, it reaches the Baḥr-i Rūm (Mediterranean) and ends at the place called Refaḥ (Rafah) where we began.... And the eastern border of Egypt extends from Baḥr-i Ḳulzüm (Red Sea) to the vicinity of Usvān (Aswan), and to ‘Ayẕāb (Aidhab), Kuṣayr (Qusayr/Quseir), Kulzüm (Suez), and the Tīh-i Benī İsrā’īl... [partial translation]
title: Refaḥ

details: FAṢL MEMLEKET-İ EFRENC VE ERMEN VE NAṢĀRĀ BEYĀNI VE ḪULEFĀ-YI MESĪḤ İ‘LĀNI ẔİKRİNDEDÜR (Section: Description of the Lands of the Franks, Armenians, and Christians, and Mention of the Successors of the Messiah): Let it not remain hidden that the ḥudūd-ı vilāyet-i Ermen (boundaries of the Armenian province) form a vast land opposite Gürcistān (Georgia).Its capital districts are Ermeniyye-i Ṣuġrā (Armenia Minor) and Ermeniyye-i Kübrā (Greater Armenia).The length (ṭūl) of Ermeniyye-i Kübrā stretches from the frontier of Āzerbaycān (Azerbaijan) to the boundary of Selmās (Salmas, Iran).Its breadth (‘arż) extends from the beginning of the Gürcistān (Georgia) province to the farthest limit of Vesṭān. As for Ermeniyye-i Ṣuġrā (Armenia Minor), its length reaches from the Syrian side (Şām ṭarafı) to the extreme frontier of the vilāyet-i Rūm (Anatolia). Likewise, its breadth runs from the frontier of Malāṭiyye (Malatya) to the border of Anṭākiyye (Antioch). All directions, regions, and mountains are included within this territory. In ancient times, there were five inhabited principal towns, which were called: Ayās (Yumurtalık, Turkey), Sīs (Kozan, Turkey), Ṭarsūs (Tarsus, Turkey), Adana (Adana, Turkey), and Misīs (Misis / Yakapınar, Turkey). All of them lie near one another. In our time, the largest of these towns is Adana. Misīs and Ayās are in ruins, while Sīs and Ṭarsūs have become towns of medium size. In former days, the region had twenty thousand inhabited villages and fertile settlements; it is reported that today no tithe (‘öşr) remains from them. Among its products: ṣūf (woollen cloth), called ḳudsī, is said to be woven in Anḳara (Ankara), which is subject to the vilāyet-i Rūm. And lāden (labdanum; fragrant resin), renowned for its delightful scent, is produced on the nearby Cezīre-i Ḳıbrıs (the Island of Cyprus). [translation]
title: Ermeniyye-i Ṣuġrā

details: On the borders of the province of Cezīre: The land of Kürdistān between Dicle (Tigris) and Furāt (Euphrates) is called Cezīre. Its western boundary extends southward along the Furāt (Euphrates) to the frontier of Malāṭiyye (Malatya), then to Samsāṭ (Samosata), and to Ḳalʿatü’r-Rūm. From there, it passes on the side of Münbic (Manbij), then to Bālīs, Raḳḳa (Raqqa), Ḳarġāmış (Carchemish), Raḥbe, Hīt, and ends at Enbār. From Enbār, it continues along the Dicle (Tigris) to Tikrīt (Tikrit), then to Sin, Ḥadīs̠e, Mevṣil (Mosul), and from there, to Cezīre-i Ibn ʿÖmer (Cizre) and reaches the city of Āmid (Diyarbakır)... details:
"...In Aſia Minor the religion is the ſame as in Turky in Europe, where only Mahometaniſm is eſtabliſhed, and Chriſtianity of all denominations and Judaiſm are barely tolerated ; ſo that the patriarchs, archbiſhops, and biſhops, whether Greeks or Armenians, as well as their ſees, churches, and congregations, are not only kept under a ſtate of deplorable poverty and ſervitude, but thoſe prelates are depoſed, changed, promoted, or oppreſſed, at the will of the ſultan and his miniſters.

The principal Greek patriarchs, beſides that of Conſtantinople, are thoſe of Jeruſalem, Alexandria, and Antioch. The Armenians have only two of them ; the firſt reſiding at Ecmeſan, a monaſtery in Georgia, and the other at Sis, in Aladulia. Beſides theſe the Neſtorians are allowed one, whose reſidence is commonly at Moſſul, in the province of Diarbeckr.

The archbiſhops belonging to the Greeks are Heraclea, Saloniki, Athens, Malvaſia, Amphipolis, Neapoli di Romania, Lariſſa, Adrianople, Corinth, Nicoſia, Janna, Monembaſia, ...(?), Phanarion, Patras, Proconeſſus, Amaſia, ...(?), Tyre, Tyana, and Berytus..."

details: Ayās: It is a port on the Baḥr-i Şām (the Syrian Sea, i.e., the eastern Mediterranean), belonging to the province of Ermen (Cilician Armenia). From there it is one-day's journey to Tell Ḥamdūn, and two-day's journey to Kūh-ı Baḳrāṣ (Mountain Baqrās) and its town. By tradition, Ayās was built by Ayās, son of Yāvān, son of Yāfeṯ, son of Noah (peace be upon him). Near it is the İskenderūne Buñarı (the Spring of Iskenderun/Alexandria), whose fortress was formerly built by Zübeyde Ḫātūn-ı Ümmü Ca‘fer. At present, the common people are still mistaken: they call that place the İskenderiyye Buñarı (“Spring of Alexandria”), which is incorrect... [partial translation]

details: Sümeysāṭ: It is a city in the aḳṣā-yı Şām (the far end of the Syrian region). It is also called Şümeysāṭ. In the time of Ḥażret-i İbrāhīm Ḫalīlu’llāh ‘aleyhi’s-selām (the Prophet Abraham, peace be upon him), there was a king of great splendor on its eastern side named Kümūs. He built Somyāṭ and Fülodyā. According to the opinion of the scholars of Bilād-ı Rey (the region of Rayy), its flourishing condition in the Islamic era occurred during the reign of Manṣūr-i ‘Abbāsī (al-Manṣūr of the Abbasids). However, after some time it again fell under the control of the Rūmīler (Byzantines). In the year 745 of the Hijra (1344 CE), Timurtaş bin Artuq conquered it, and it was firmly established that the city came under the rule of the Artuqids. [translation]

details: FAṢL MEMLEKET-İ EFRENC VE ERMEN VE NAṢĀRĀ BEYĀNI VE ḪULEFĀ-YI MESĪḤ İ‘LĀNI ẔİKRİNDEDÜR (Section: Description of the Lands of the Franks, Armenians, and Christians, and Mention of the Successors of the Messiah): Let it not remain hidden that the ḥudūd-ı vilāyet-i Ermen (boundaries of the Armenian province) form a vast land opposite Gürcistān (Georgia).Its capital districts are Ermeniyye-i Ṣuġrā (Armenia Minor) and Ermeniyye-i Kübrā (Greater Armenia).The length (ṭūl) of Ermeniyye-i Kübrā stretches from the frontier of Āzerbaycān (Azerbaijan) to the boundary of Selmās (Salmas, Iran).Its breadth (‘arż) extends from the beginning of the Gürcistān (Georgia) province to the farthest limit of Vesṭān. As for Ermeniyye-i Ṣuġrā (Armenia Minor), its length reaches from the Syrian side (Şām ṭarafı) to the extreme frontier of the vilāyet-i Rūm (Anatolia). Likewise, its breadth runs from the frontier of Malāṭiyye (Malatya) to the border of Anṭākiyye (Antioch). All directions, regions, and mountains are included within this territory. In ancient times, there were five inhabited principal towns, which were called: Ayās (Yumurtalık, Turkey), Sīs (Kozan, Turkey), Ṭarsūs (Tarsus, Turkey), Adana (Adana, Turkey), and Misīs (Misis / Yakapınar, Turkey). All of them lie near one another. In our time, the largest of these towns is Adana. Misīs and Ayās are in ruins, while Sīs and Ṭarsūs have become towns of medium size. In former days, the region had twenty thousand inhabited villages and fertile settlements; it is reported that today no tithe (‘öşr) remains from them. Among its products: ṣūf (woollen cloth), called ḳudsī, is said to be woven in Anḳara (Ankara), which is subject to the vilāyet-i Rūm. And lāden (labdanum; fragrant resin), renowned for its delightful scent, is produced on the nearby Cezīre-i Ḳıbrıs (the Island of Cyprus). [translation]
title: Misīs

details: "ATRA, (mentioned under the article ARRA) a city of the Arraceni, or Saracens, in Arabia, but the exact situation of it is not determined, at least that we can find. When the emperor Trajan marched into Arabia, and there made war upon the Arraceni, or Hagareni, he laid siege to their city which by Xiphilin is called Atra. It was neither great nor beautiful, says Dion Cassius, but thought to be very rich, by reason the sun was worshipped there, which drew crouds of people thither with rich presents from the neighbouring countries. It was situated on the top of a high and steep mountain, well peopled, and surrounded with strong walls. But its chief strength consisted in the barrenness of the neighbouring country, destitute to a great distance of grass, wood, and even of water, so that a great army could not long subsist before it. Hence it was neither taken now by Trajan, nor afterwards by Severus, though they had both made a breach in the wall. Trajan narrowly escaped being killed in one of the attacks. The Romans were moreover infested, in their camp, in a strange manner, by swarms of flies; so that Trajan in the end was obliged to raise the siege and retire." (Seally, 1787, Vol. 1, s.v. “Atra”)
title: Atra

details: On the borders of the province of Cezīre: The land of Kürdistān between Dicle (Tigris) and Furāt (Euphrates) is called Cezīre. Its western boundary extends southward along the Furāt (Euphrates) to the frontier of Malāṭiyye (Malatya), then to Samsāṭ (Samosata), and to Ḳalʿatü’r-Rūm. From there, it passes on the side of Münbic (Manbij), then to Bālīs, Raḳḳa (Raqqa), Ḳarġāmış (Carchemish), Raḥbe, Hīt, and ends at Enbār. From Enbār, it continues along the Dicle (Tigris) to Tikrīt (Tikrit), then to Sin, Ḥadīs̠e, Mevṣil (Mosul), and from there, to Cezīre-i Ibn ʿÖmer (Cizre) and reaches the city of Āmid (Diyarbakır)... (partially translated by the first creator of this entry.)

details:
"...In Aſia Minor the religion is the ſame as in Turky in Europe, where only Mahometaniſm is eſtabliſhed, and Chriſtianity of all denominations and Judaiſm are barely tolerated ; ſo that the patriarchs, archbiſhops, and biſhops, whether Greeks or Armenians, as well as their ſees, churches, and congregations, are not only kept under a ſtate of deplorable poverty and ſervitude, but thoſe prelates are depoſed, changed, promoted, or oppreſſed, at the will of the ſultan and his miniſters.

The principal Greek patriarchs, beſides that of Conſtantinople, are thoſe of Jeruſalem, Alexandria, and Antioch. The Armenians have only two of them ; the firſt reſiding at Ecmeſan, a monaſtery in Georgia, and the other at Sis, in Aladulia. Beſides theſe the Neſtorians are allowed one, whose reſidence is commonly at Moſſul, in the province of Diarbeckr.

The archbiſhops belonging to the Greeks are Heraclea, Saloniki, Athens, Malvaſia, Amphipolis, Neapoli di Romania, Lariſſa, Adrianople, Corinth, Nicoſia, Janna, Monembaſia, ...(?), Phanarion, Patras, Proconeſſus, Amaſia, ...(?), Tyre, Tyana, and Berytus..."

details: "AMIDA, a great city of Mesopotamia, or Ammæ; situated on a high mountain on the borders of Assyria, on the Tigris, where it receives the Nymphius. It was taken from the Romans in the time of the emperor Constans by Sapores, king of Persia. The siege is said to have cost him 30,000 men; however, he reduced it to such ruin that the emperor afterwards wept over it. According to Ammianus Marcellinus, the city was razed; the chief officers were crucified; and the rest, with the soldiers and inhabitants, either put to the sword or carried into captivity, except our historian himself, and two or three more, who, in the dead of the night, escaped through a postern unperceived by the enemy. The inhabitants of Nisibis, however, being obliged to leave their own city by Jovian's treaty with the Persians, soon restored Amida to its former strength; but it was again taken by Cavades in 501, but was restored to the Romans in 503. On the declension of the Roman power it fell again into the hands of the Persians; but was taken from them by the Saracens in 809. It is now in the possession of the Turks. Here are above 20,000 Christians, who are better treated by the Turks than in other places. A great trade is carried on in this city of red Turkey leather, and cotton cloth of the same colour. The Arabian name of Amida is Diarbekir, and the Turkish one Kara-Amed. Long. 39. 0. E. Lat. 36, 58, N." (Seally, 1787, Vol. 1, entry Amida)
title: Amida

details:
"...In Aſia Minor the religion is the ſame as in Turky in Europe, where only Mahometaniſm is eſtabliſhed, and Chriſtianity of all denominations and Judaiſm are barely tolerated ; ſo that the patriarchs, archbiſhops, and biſhops, whether Greeks or Armenians, as well as their ſees, churches, and congregations, are not only kept under a ſtate of deplorable poverty and ſervitude, but thoſe prelates are depoſed, changed, promoted, or oppreſſed, at the will of the ſultan and his miniſters.

The principal Greek patriarchs, beſides that of Conſtantinople, are thoſe of Jeruſalem, Alexandria, and Antioch. The Armenians have only two of them ; the firſt reſiding at Ecmeſan, a monaſtery in Georgia, and the other at Sis, in Aladulia. Beſides theſe the Neſtorians are allowed one, whose reſidence is commonly at Moſſul, in the province of Diarbeckr.

The archbiſhops belonging to the Greeks are Heraclea, Saloniki, Athens, Malvaſia, Amphipolis, Neapoli di Romania, Lariſſa, Adrianople, Corinth, Nicoſia, Janna, Monembaſia, ...(?), Phanarion, Patras, Proconeſſus, Amaſia, ...(?), Tyre, Tyana, and Berytus..."
title: Diarbeckr

details: On the borders of the province of Cezīre: The land of Kürdistān between Dicle (Tigris) and Furāt (Euphrates) is called Cezīre. Its western boundary extends southward along the Furāt (Euphrates) to the frontier of Malāṭiyye (Malatya), then to Samsāṭ (Samosata), and to Ḳalʿatü’r-Rūm. From there, it passes on the side of Münbic (Manbij), then to Bālīs, Raḳḳa (Raqqa), Ḳarġāmış (Carchemish), Raḥbe, Hīt, and ends at Enbār. From Enbār, it continues along the Dicle (Tigris) to Tikrīt (Tikrit), then to Sin, Ḥadīs̠e, Mevṣil (Mosul), and from there, to Cezīre-i Ibn ʿÖmer (Cizre) and reaches the city of Āmid (Diyarbakır)... (partially translated by the first creator of this entry.)
title: Cezīre-i İbn ʿÖmer

details: Buḥayre-i Tilā: Another name for it is Buḥayre-i Urmiye (Lake Urmia). It lies between Merā‘a (Maragheh) and Selmās (Salmas). Its length extends for about one hundred and thirty miles, but the distance of its full circuit is expressed as a six-day journey. In its middle there is an island, and on that island stands a fortress called Tilā. When Hülāgū Ḫān (Hulagu Khan) gained dominion over those lands, he placed his treasures and wealth for safekeeping there and appointed each year one thousand armed guards to protect it. At the end of every year, another thousand men would be sent to replace them. [translation]

details: FAṢL MEMLEKET-İ EFRENC VE ERMEN VE NAṢĀRĀ BEYĀNI VE ḪULEFĀ-YI MESĪḤ İ‘LĀNI ẔİKRİNDEDÜR (Section: Description of the Lands of the Franks, Armenians, and Christians, and Mention of the Successors of the Messiah): Let it not remain hidden that the ḥudūd-ı vilāyet-i Ermen (boundaries of the Armenian province) form a vast land opposite Gürcistān (Georgia).Its capital districts are Ermeniyye-i Ṣuġrā (Armenia Minor) and Ermeniyye-i Kübrā (Greater Armenia).The length (ṭūl) of Ermeniyye-i Kübrā stretches from the frontier of Āzerbaycān (Azerbaijan) to the boundary of Selmās (Salmas, Iran).Its breadth (‘arż) extends from the beginning of the Gürcistān (Georgia) province to the farthest limit of Vesṭān. As for Ermeniyye-i Ṣuġrā (Armenia Minor), its length reaches from the Syrian side (Şām ṭarafı) to the extreme frontier of the vilāyet-i Rūm (Anatolia). Likewise, its breadth runs from the frontier of Malāṭiyye (Malatya) to the border of Anṭākiyye (Antioch). All directions, regions, and mountains are included within this territory. In ancient times, there were five inhabited principal towns, which were called: Ayās (Yumurtalık, Turkey), Sīs (Kozan, Turkey), Ṭarsūs (Tarsus, Turkey), Adana (Adana, Turkey), and Misīs (Misis / Yakapınar, Turkey). All of them lie near one another. In our time, the largest of these towns is Adana. Misīs and Ayās are in ruins, while Sīs and Ṭarsūs have become towns of medium size. In former days, the region had twenty thousand inhabited villages and fertile settlements; it is reported that today no tithe (‘öşr) remains from them. Among its products: ṣūf (woollen cloth), called ḳudsī, is said to be woven in Anḳara (Ankara), which is subject to the vilāyet-i Rūm. And lāden (labdanum; fragrant resin), renowned for its delightful scent, is produced on the nearby Cezīre-i Ḳıbrıs (the Island of Cyprus). [translation]
title: Ermeniyye-i Kübrā

details: Nehr-i İs̱īl: It is as big as the Tigris. It flows from the lands of Rūm and Bulgar to the lands of the Khazars. According to the scholars, it eventually pours again into the Khazar Sea. Particularly, seventy-five rivers branch off from it, yet it neither decreases nor changes. Even after it joins the sea, it continues to flow for a distance of two days clearly; it does not change its color. It doesn't change its appearance. In the sea, it can be easily distinguished. Moreover, in the winter season, it freezes. It includes peculiar types of aquatic animals. (Translated from Ottoman Turkish to English by the first creator of the name.)

details:
"...In Aſia Minor the religion is the ſame as in Turky in Europe, where only Mahometaniſm is eſtabliſhed, and Chriſtianity of all denominations and Judaiſm are barely tolerated ; ſo that the patriarchs, archbiſhops, and biſhops, whether Greeks or Armenians, as well as their ſees, churches, and congregations, are not only kept under a ſtate of deplorable poverty and ſervitude, but thoſe prelates are depoſed, changed, promoted, or oppreſſed, at the will of the ſultan and his miniſters.

The principal Greek patriarchs, beſides that of Conſtantinople, are thoſe of Jeruſalem, Alexandria, and Antioch. The Armenians have only two of them ; the firſt reſiding at Ecmeſan, a monaſtery in Georgia, and the other at Sis, in Aladulia. Beſides theſe the Neſtorians are allowed one, whose reſidence is commonly at Moſſul, in the province of Diarbeckr.

The archbiſhops belonging to the Greeks are Heraclea, Saloniki, Athens, Malvaſia, Amphipolis, Neapoli di Romania, Lariſſa, Adrianople, Corinth, Nicoſia, Janna, Monembaſia, ...(?), Phanarion, Patras, Proconeſſus, Amaſia, ...(?), Tyre, Tyana, and Berytus..."

details: Der-ḥudūd-i Filisṭīn: It is a large district, within which lie Beytü’l-maḳdis (Jerusalem), Ġazze (Gaza), and ‘Asḳalān (Ashkelon). Its western boundary runs from Refaḥ (Rafah) to Leccūn (Legio), and its width is two days’ journey, extending from Yāfā (Jaffa) to Erīḥā (Jericho). At present, Zuġar, the diyār-ı Lūṭ (the region of Lot, i.e., around the Dead Sea), as well as Cibāl and Şerrān (the Sharon plain) are all attached to Filisṭīn (Palestine). Its water comes from rainfall, except in Nāblus (Nablus), where there is running water. And the great cities of this ‘örfī (customary administrative) district are Beyt-i Maḳdis (Jerusalem), Ġazze (Gaza), and Remle (Ramla). Allāh knows the best. details: Nehr-i Nīl (Nile River): ... After this, from the Nīl-i Mıṣr (Nile of Egypt), the Nehr-i Feyyūm (Fayyum River / Bahr Yussef Canal) branches off. When its waters increase, it reaches the Nehr-i Sūs-i Aḳṣā (the Far Sūs River / possibly the Oued Souss in Morocco). The Nehr-i Sūs (Souss River) descends from the Cebel-i Lemṭa. It passes through the city of Sūs (Souss) and flows north of it. On its shores grow abundant sugarcane (ḳaṣab-ı sükker) and henna (ḥınnā). That is, just as the produce of the regions around the Nile is obtained from it, so too is produce taken from the River Sūs. Afterwards, it flows into the sea. [partial translation]

details:
Capua was founded approximately 600 BCE by the Etruscans.  In the following years, it quickly gained power over local communities such as Casilinum, Calatia, and Atella.  Capua was later taken over by the Samnites in 440 BCE.  In 340 BCE, the populace of Capua supported the Latin Confederacy against Rome, but ended up losing the war.  Rome made Capua into a municipium, granting its citizens Roman citizenship without the right to vote in elections.  This allowed Capua to remain self-governed.  It became connected to Rome through the Via Appia in 312 BCE, making it one of the most powerful cities in Italy in terms of trading and population.  In terms of trading, it was most well known for its bronzes, and perfumes such as seplasium.  Capua was called "Altera Roma" by Cicero because of the wealth and opulence the city became known for.

Capua sided against the Romans once again in the Second Punic War.  Livy believed Capua to be Hannibal's own "Cannae", as the luxurious conditions of the city may have softened his troops.  Capua was recaptured in 211 BCE.  As punishment, the Romans rescinded their citizenship rights and their self-governance was replaced with being ruled over by Roman prefects.  As was often the case with recent Roman conquests, settlements were founded nearby; two such settlements, called Volternum and Liternum, were founded in 194 BCE.  

Capua was perhaps most known for its gladiatorial games.  The city was home to the second largest amphitheater in Italy (following the Colosseum) and could hold as many as 60,000 spectators.  Many gladiatorial schools (ludi) were situated in Capua and produced some of the greatest gladiators in the Republic.  The largest ludus in the Republic, belonging to Lentulus Batiatus, produced Spartacus and his followers who went on to organize one of the largest slave revolts in history in 73 BCE.

Capua, though a Roman stronghold throughout the reign of the empire, fell in 456 CE when it was invaded by the Vandals under their leader Genseric.  The little that was left standing in this ancient city was destroyed by Muslim invaders approximately four hundred years later around 840 CE.  The town that currently stands in its place is Santa Maria Capua Vetere, named for the sole church the Muslim invaders spared.
title: Capua

details:
Yet Baḥr-i Hind: it also has another name, Baḥr-i Aḫḍar (the Green Sea). Its eastern side borders the lands of Ṣīn (China), and its northern side adjoins the fertile regions of Hind (India). Its western side reaches the lands of Yemen, but its southern extent is unknown to far-seeing minds, and as it stretches onward, it passes by the Cezīre-i Serendīb (the Island of Serendib; modern Sri Lanka). It is reported that in the Baḥr-i Ṣīn (the China Sea), which is connected to the Indian Ocean, there are one thousand seven hundred inhabited islands, each with abundant populations. Besides these, it is said that the uninhabited islands are innumerable and beyond all reckoning. In general, another name of the Deryā-yı Hind (Indian Ocean) is Baḥr-i Zenc (the Sea of the Zanj/Africans), for the lands of Zenc (Zanj, the East African coast) lie to its south, and thus it came to be called the Sea of Zanj. It is connected to the Baḥr-i Muḥīṭ (the Great Ocean / the surrounding ocean).

There is no sea whose waves, surges, and tumults make such terrifying and astonishing noises. However, it does not foam, nor does its sand crack upon contact; otherwise, ships could never pass through that sea. Waves of that kind have been described as mevc-i mecnūn (crazy waves)... [partial translation]

details: Baḥr-i Fārs (Persian Gulf): It is a sea that emerges from the northern side of the Baḥr-i Hind (Indian Ocean). To the east of Mekrāntīz (Makran coast region), at the source of the Baḥr-i Fārs, it appears visibly like a mouth (dehān). Likewise, the city of ‘Ummān (Oman) is seen on the western side of this sea, and it too is discernible at its mouth, that is, its strait. From there it extends, running along the ‘Ummān (Oman) coast, and from ‘Abbādān (Abadan, Iran) to Mehrūbān (Mahrūbān, near modern Bushehr). Then it passes to Sīnīz (modern Bushehr/Old Siniz) and stretches southward until it reaches Ḫayyābe (Khabbah / Khaybah). From there it proceeds to Seyfü’l-baḥr (“the Sword of the Sea,” Fars coast), and to its east is Sīrāf (Siraf, Iran). From that point, it continues along broken mountain ranges and high desert passes and hills, and then, moving further east, it winds around to Ḥıṣn Ibn ‘Ammāre (Hisn Ibn ‘Ammāra) and reaches Hürmüz (Hormuz), which is the port of Kirmān (Kerman). After that, it stretches toward the southeastern direction, reaching the Makran coast and Ḳaṣṣatīz. [translation]
title: Sīrāf

details: Atyantakāma-pallaveśvara-gṛha is attested as the name of several seventh-century Pallava rock-cut and cave temples in Mahābalipuram. It is thus not to be excluded that Atyantakāma-pallaveśvara-gṛha is a later name of the original foundation, given not long after the actual foundation. The original name of the temple, if any, is unknown.

details: Nehr-i Sūs: It flows above the city called İstanca (Istanja / Écija, Spain). The inhabitants of the villages along its banks engage in abundant agriculture. It descends from the cibāl-i Şuġūre (Mountains of Shughur / Sierra Morena) toward Cühelācinān (Jūhala–Cinān? a region in al-Andalus), then passes by the cities of Yebāt (Ébora / Evora?) and Ḳurṭuba (Córdoba). To the east, it reaches İşbiliyye (Seville); to the west, it passes by Ṭırmāna (Tirmana?) and finally flows into the Baḥr-i Muḥīṭ (the Atlantic Ocean). In this river, just as in the Dicle (Tigris) near Basra, tides (medd u cezr) occur. It is said that during the tidal period, the water advances seventy miles, and even then its water does not become salty, but remains fresh. The more the moon’s light increases, the greater the rising tide becomes. Ships set out for their destinations at this favorable moment. Sometimes, Frankish ships enter this river from the Baḥr-i Muḥīṭ (Atlantic) and sail as far as İşbiliyye (Seville). [translation]
title: Cibāl-i Şuġūre

details: Nehr-i Sūs: It flows above the city called İstanca (Istanja / Écija, Spain). The inhabitants of the villages along its banks engage in abundant agriculture. It descends from the cibāl-i Şuġūre (Mountains of Shughur / Sierra Morena) toward Cühelācinān (Jūhala–Cinān? a region in al-Andalus), then passes by the cities of Yebāt (Ébora / Evora?) and Ḳurṭuba (Córdoba). To the east, it reaches İşbiliyye (Seville); to the west, it passes by Ṭırmāna (Tirmana?) and finally flows into the Baḥr-i Muḥīṭ (the Atlantic Ocean). In this river, just as in the Dicle (Tigris) near Basra, tides (medd u cezr) occur. It is said that during the tidal period, the water advances seventy miles, and even then its water does not become salty, but remains fresh. The more the moon’s light increases, the greater the rising tide becomes. Ships set out for their destinations at this favorable moment. Sometimes, Frankish ships enter this river from the Baḥr-i Muḥīṭ (Atlantic) and sail as far as İşbiliyye (Seville). [translation]
title: İstanca

"...In Aſia Minor the religion is the ſame as in Turky in Europe, where only Mahometaniſm is eſtabliſhed, and Chriſtianity of all denominations and Judaiſm are barely tolerated ; ſo that the patriarchs, archbiſhops, and biſhops, whether Greeks or Armenians, as well as their ſees, churches, and congregations, are not only kept under a ſtate of deplorable poverty and ſervitude, but thoſe prelates are depoſed, changed, promoted, or oppreſſed, at the will of the ſultan and his miniſters.

The principal Greek patriarchs, beſides that of Conſtantinople, are thoſe of Jeruſalem, Alexandria, and Antioch. The Armenians have only two of them ; the firſt reſiding at Ecmeſan, a monaſtery in Georgia, and the other at Sis, in Aladulia. Beſides theſe the Neſtorians are allowed one, whose reſidence is commonly at Moſſul, in the province of Diarbeckr.

The archbiſhops belonging to the Greeks are Heraclea, Saloniki, Athens, Malvaſia, Amphipolis, Neapoli di Romania, Lariſſa, Adrianople, Corinth, Nicoſia, Janna, Monembaſia, ...(?), Phanarion, Patras, Proconeſſus, Amaſia, ...(?), Tyre, Tyana, and Berytus..."

details:
Cezā’ir-i Serendīb: Eni ve uzunı seksen fersaḫdur. Ehl-i Hind ḳavlince Ḥażret-i Ādem ‘aleyhi’s-selām ol cezīredeki ṭaġlaruñ birine inmişdür. Ekābir-i Berāhime taḥḳīḳi üzere Ḥażret-i Ādem’üñ ḳademi yiri anda henüz ma‘lūmdur. Ḥattā yetmiş ẕirā‘ uzunında maġmūs u mersūmdür. Gicede ve gündüzde ol ṭaġ üzerinde nūr gibi bir żiyā ẓāhir olur. Ba‘de-mā Ḥażret-i Ādem ol cezīreden iki adım inmişdür, didükleri iki günlik mesāfedür. Fe-lā-cerem anuñ ḥavālīsi eṣnāf-ı cevāhirle memlūdur. Ve la‘l ü elmās u yāḳūtla [69b E] müzeyyen ve ṭopṭoludur.

Islands of Serendib: Its length and width are eighty farsakhs. According to the people of India, Prophet Adam (peace be upon him) landed on one of the mountains on this island. According to the accounts of the knowledgeable Brahmans, the place where Prophet Adam set foot is still known; Also, its foot size is about seventy cubits long. A light like a luminous glow appears on that mountation during day and night. It is also said that after descending from the island, Prophet Adam took two steps and each step corresponds to a distance of one day journey for human. For this reason, the surrounding area is rich with various kinds of gems. Also, it is decorated and full with rubies, diamonds, and sapphires. (Translation provided by the creator of this entry)
title: Cezā’ir-i Serendīb

details: "CERIGO, anciently Cythera [sic], an island in the Candian Sea, and European Turky, between Candia and the Morea, about 50 miles N. of the former, and near the E. part of the latter. It is a mountainous rocky country, which yields but very little corn, wine, or oil, and has not a great number of inhabitants. The principal town lies on the S. side of the island, and on a dreadful precipice stands a castle, but the harbour under it is exposed to S. winds. This island was anciently dedicated to Venus, whose native country it was; as also of Helen, the occasion of the siege and destruction of Troy. Lat. 36, 5, N.; Long. 23, 40, E." (Seally, 1787, Vol. 1, s.v. “Cerigo”)

details: "DIVIN, a castle in the Hither Circle of the Danube, in Lower Hungary, upon a very steep rock. In 1576 it was taken by the Turks, who kept it till 1593. In the year 1674, it was taken from the rebels Balassa, and demolished; so that at present it is no more than a heap of rubbish. From it a place in the neighbourhood takes its name, in whose jurisdiction it stands. The inhabitants employ themselves in agriculture and hunting." (Seally, 1787, s.v. “Vidin”)
